THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Ibn Battuta’s Twenty-Nine Years Across the Afro-Eurasian World

Leaving Tangier at twenty-one in 1325 CE, Maliki scholar Muhammad ibn Battuta crossed an interconnected hemispheric world where Arabic jurisprudence, caravanserai endowments, and monsoon dhows linked Moroccan mosques with Indian Ocean sultanates and West African Niger capitals.

Connects primary textual testimony dictated to Ibn Juzayy in Fez (1355–1356 CE) with dated architectural, numismatic, and port excavations at Cairo, Mogadishu, Kilwa, Delhi, Quanzhou, and Mali.

An institutional world before national borders

Throughout the fourteenth century, trained scholars carried portable Maliki and Shafi‘i legal credentials along overland post-roads and seasonal maritime fleets from Andalusia to Southeast Asia. Wherever mosque endowments and merchant hostels existed, jurists could step directly into salaried judgeships and ambassadorial offices. [1] [2]

In East Africa (Zeila, Mogadishu, Mombasa, and Kilwa) and later the Maldives and coastal Sumatra, Ibn Battuta recorded how Islamic courtly etiquette braided seamlessly with Swahili stone urbanism, cowrie currencies, and local matrilineal traditions. [3] [4]

Corroborating memory and hindsight in the Rihla

Dictated without continuous ship logs after returning to Fez around 1354 CE, the Rihla blends remarkable eyewitness precision—names of obscure provincial governors confirmed by inscriptions in Pasai and Malé—with telescoped chronology on northern excursions to Bulgar or Khanbaliq. [1] [2]

Archaeology and inscriptions corroborating fourteenth-century routes

Standing coral-rag palaces and vaulted baths at Kilwa Kisiwani match Ibn Battuta’s 1331 CE description of Sultan Abu al-Mawahib’s court, while royal funerary inscriptions in Pasai and Maldivian chronicle synchronisms anchor his Indian Ocean passage in independent material evidence. [3] [4] [1]
